title: P–P plots: compare observed probabilities with a fixed reference CDF
summary: Construct a probability–probability plot with an explicit plotting-position rule, then read its center and tail limits without confusing it with a Q–Q plot.
body:
Construct a probability–probability plot with an explicit plotting-position rule, then read its center and tail limits without confusing it with a Q–Q plot.

Ask a probability-scale question

A P–P plot checks whether an observed distribution agrees with a specified cumulative distribution function. Sort the observations. For each ordered value, put the reference CDF probability on one axis and an empirical plotting position on the other. If the two distributions agree, the points follow the diagonal within sampling variation. Both axes run from zero to one, so the coordinates are comparable across measurement units. This is a descriptive diagnostic, not a certificate that a model is correct. State which axis carries which probability: the sign of a deviation reverses if the axes are swapped. A persistent arc above the diagonal means the empirical cumulative share exceeds the proposed reference at those thresholds; it does not by itself name a physical cause. Empirical CDFs show the same cumulative story against measured values, while Q–Q plots put values rather than probabilities on the axes.

Fix the reference before inspection

Choose the reference distribution and its parameters from an external specification, an earlier frozen baseline or a fitting procedure whose use is declared. If mean and spread are estimated from the same sample, the resulting P–P points are drawn closer to the reference by construction; a line that looks good is then weaker evidence. Fitting after spotting a discrepancy compounds the problem. For a fresh validation set, keep the baseline version and population definition fixed. The worked contract uses a normal reference with a predeclared center of 71 and spread of 20. A normal CDF can assign probability to impossible negative values when the underlying measure cannot be negative, so choose a reference family consistent with the measurement domain. The plot should carry the exact center, spread, sample count and reference revision. Chart export metadata and unit-of-analysis rules make that comparison repeatable.

Declare a plotting position and treat ties honestly

For N sorted observations this lesson uses the midpoint position (rank minus one half) divided by N. It stays inside the open interval and gives every observation one ordinate. Other conventions are valid, but changing conventions moves the endpoints, especially when N is small. If measured values tie because a sensor rounds to whole units, several observations share a reference-CDF coordinate while their plotting positions differ. That vertical run is data, not a rendering error. If the reference has discrete jumps, the continuous midpoint convention requires a more careful discrete diagnostic; do not interpret the diagonal with continuous-case intuition. Missing, infinite and mixed-unit values must be resolved before sorting. Histograms can reveal rounding and mass points that a probability plot hides, and small-sample guidance keeps isolated deviations in perspective.

Know what a probability scale suppresses

Because both axes are bounded by zero and one, P–P plots are often easy to read through the center of a distribution. They compress extreme-value differences: a large change in the far tail may correspond to a tiny probability change near zero or one. Use a Q–Q plot or an explicit tail exceedance display when the operating decision depends on rare extreme values. Do not silently crop the first and last points; doing so makes a bad fit look quieter. Keep a square plotting region, equal numeric scales and a visible forty-five-degree reference line. An accessible companion table can list measured threshold, proposed CDF, empirical position and their difference. For two populations, use comparable panels or a stated two-sample construction rather than passing one estimated empirical CDF off as an independent fixed standard. Shared-scale panels and text alternatives preserve the evidence.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite
from statistics import NormalDist

def probability_probability_points(
    response_ms: list[float], reference_center: float,
    reference_spread: float,
):
    if (not response_ms or not isfinite(reference_center) or
            not isfinite(reference_spread) or reference_spread <= 0 or
            any(not isfinite(value) for value in response_ms)):
        raise ValueError("finite observations and a positive reference spread are required")
    reference = NormalDist(mu=reference_center, sigma=reference_spread)
    ordered = sorted(response_ms)
    sample_size = len(ordered)
    return [(value, reference.cdf(value), (rank - 0.5) / sample_size)
            for rank, value in enumerate(ordered, start=1)]

latency_sample = [59.0, 71.0, 83.0, 71.0, 97.0]
points = probability_probability_points(latency_sample, 71.0, 20.0)
assert [row[0] for row in points] == [59.0, 71.0, 71.0, 83.0, 97.0]
assert [row[2] for row in points] == [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]
assert points[1][1] == points[2][1] == 0.5
assert points[0][1] < 0.5 < points[-1][1]

Performance and operating cost

For N observations, validation is O(N), sorting is O(N log N), and one reference-CDF evaluation per row is O(N) under the standard constant-cost numerical model. The returned ledger and sorted copy require O(N) space. The five-value arithmetic check includes a repeated 71-millisecond reading: two points share reference probability 0.5 but occupy different empirical positions, 0.3 and 0.5. Five records are not enough to judge distributional fit; gather a representative, independently selected validation sample before interpreting the shape. A displayed diagonal is an expected relationship, not a formal acceptance test or a confidence band.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a P–P plot a Q–Q plot while labeling its axes in measurement units.
  • Estimating reference parameters on the inspection sample without disclosing the fit.
  • Treating tied measured values as duplicates to delete before assigning ranks.
  • Using center-focused visual agreement to dismiss a consequential extreme tail.

Validation drill

Freeze a 71-millisecond center and 20-millisecond spread from a prior release. Plot 83 new, independently selected response times using midpoint positions; include an accessible table and compare the tail diagnosis with a Q–Q plot before changing the reference.

title: Wind roses: map direction, speed and calm conditions without losing the denominator
summary: Bin directional observations across the north boundary, retain calm and missing readings separately, and report sector shares with a clear speed-band contract.
body:
Bin directional observations across the north boundary, retain calm and missing readings separately, and report sector shares with a clear speed-band contract.

Write down what a direction means

A wind rose summarizes how often wind arrived from each compass sector, often subdivided by speed. In meteorological usage, a north reading means air came from the north; an arrow showing where the air travels points south. Confusing origin with travel direction rotates the interpretation by half a circle. Other directional datasets, such as vehicle headings, may use the direction of travel instead, so the chart title must say which convention applies. Angles wrap: 359 degrees and 1 degree belong next to each other, not at opposite ends of a linear axis. Choose a compass origin, clockwise ordering and sector count before grouping. With eight equal sectors, a north-centered bin covers angles near both zero and 360 degrees. Encoding choices and wrapped coordinates explain why a straight numeric interval can be misleading here.

Separate calm from missing and invalid

When wind speed falls below a declared calm threshold, direction is physically uninformative or not reported. Give calm observations a separate count and share. A missing direction with a measurable wind speed is a data-quality issue, not calm. A missing speed is another quality issue. Decide whether the reporting denominator includes all valid measured periods, calm plus directional periods, or only non-calm directional periods, and put that choice beside every percentage. Comparing two stations using different calm thresholds changes the result even if their actual wind conditions match. Time spacing also matters: ten readings captured in one busy hour should not carry the same meaning as ten evenly spaced hours if the goal is time exposure. The example assumes one equally weighted observation per scheduled time slot and rejects malformed data. Denominator policy and missing-period rules must be fixed before charting.

Keep speed bands and radial scale explicit

A sector wedge can be divided into speed bands, but its total must reconcile to the number of qualifying observations in that sector. Use one speed unit throughout, non-overlapping boundaries and a named rule for observations exactly on a boundary. Here bands are below 6, from 6 through less than 14, and 14 or above, in metres per second. The code places a value of exactly 6 into the middle band. Label whether radius encodes count, percent of all valid periods, or percent within a sector. These answer different questions. If wedge angle is fixed, radial length is easy to compare but geometric area grows with its square; do not say area represents frequency unless the rendering actually uses an area-correct transform. Give a companion table of sector totals, band counts and shares. Area encoding and accessible alternatives cover those distinctions.

Compare stations on matched exposure

A rose from one winter month should not be compared casually with a full-year rose from another location. Align the observation window, sampling cadence, sensor height and missingness policy. Report the number of eligible time slots and the share excluded for missing readings; a direction bias can be produced by a sensor that drops out during storms. A wind rose aggregates away sequence. A short storm and recurring moderate winds may occupy the same direction sector but have different operational meaning. For an exposure or safety decision, pair the rose with a time-series chart and separate gust statistics. Do not infer local causes from sector frequencies alone. Seasonal subseries can expose changing seasonal patterns, while small multiples keep station comparisons on a common radial scale.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

SECTORS = ("N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW")

def wind_rose_ledger(readings: list[tuple[str, float | None, float | None]],
                     calm_below: float = 1.0):
    if not isfinite(calm_below) or calm_below < 0:
        raise ValueError("calm threshold must be finite and nonnegative")
    sector_bands = [[0, 0, 0] for _ in SECTORS]
    seen_slots = set()
    calm = missing = 0
    for slot_id, direction_from_degrees, speed_mps in readings:
        if not slot_id or slot_id in seen_slots:
            raise ValueError("each scheduled slot needs a unique ID")
        seen_slots.add(slot_id)
        if speed_mps is None or direction_from_degrees is None:
            missing += 1
            continue
        if (not isfinite(speed_mps) or speed_mps < 0 or
                not isfinite(direction_from_degrees) or
                not 0 <= direction_from_degrees < 360):
            raise ValueError("speed and direction must use declared units")
        if speed_mps < calm_below:
            calm += 1
            continue
        sector = int((direction_from_degrees + 22.5) // 45) % 8
        band = 0 if speed_mps < 6 else 1 if speed_mps < 14 else 2
        sector_bands[sector][band] += 1
    measured = len(readings) - missing
    if measured == 0:
        raise ValueError("no measured slots")
    directional = sum(sum(bands) for bands in sector_bands)
    assert directional + calm == measured
    return {
        "measured": measured, "missing": missing, "calm": calm,
        "calm_share": calm / measured,
        "sector_bands": dict(zip(SECTORS, sector_bands)),
    }

hourly_readings = [("hour-47", 359.0, 5.0), ("hour-48", 1.0, 6.0),
                   ("hour-49", 47.0, 14.0), ("hour-50", 271.0, 0.4),
                   ("hour-51", None, 9.0)]
rose = wind_rose_ledger(hourly_readings)
assert rose["sector_bands"]["N"] == [1, 1, 0]
assert rose["sector_bands"]["NE"] == [0, 0, 1]
assert (rose["measured"], rose["calm"], rose["missing"]) == (4, 1, 1)
assert rose["calm_share"] == 0.25

Performance and operating cost

For N scheduled readings, validation and accumulation take O(N) expected time; the slot-ID set uses O(N) space, while the fixed eight-by-three tally uses O(1). The example groups 359 and 1 degrees into north, assigns exactly 6 metres per second to the middle speed band, and counts a measured low-speed west reading as calm. Four measured hours form the denominator, so calm share is 25 percent. The fifth scheduled hour is missing, not calm. A real deployment should monitor missing-share changes and may need duration weighting when observation intervals are unequal.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading meteorological wind direction as the direction air travels toward.
  • Placing angles near zero and 360 degrees in distant bins.
  • Converting missing directions into calm readings or silently dropping them from every count.
  • Comparing roses with different sampling windows, calm thresholds or radial denominators.

Validation drill

Build a rose for 83 scheduled hourly slots from a sensor log. Reconcile directional, calm and missing counts, document the direction convention and speed units, then compare two matched seasons using the same sectors and radial scale.

  • Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
  • Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order

title: Q–Q plots: compare distribution shape beyond one summary number
summary: Pair probabilities rather than row positions, state the reference distribution and inspect tail behavior separately.
body:
Pair probabilities rather than row positions, state the reference distribution and inspect tail behavior separately.

A quantile is an ordered position

A Q–Q plot compares quantiles from two distributions at the same cumulative probabilities. It does not pair individual records, even if both samples have the same size. State whether the horizontal axis is an observed reference group or a theoretical distribution, and label units on both axes. ECDF and percentile reading provide the underlying probability view. A line of points near a diagonal suggests broadly similar locations and spreads only if both axes use the same unit and scale; otherwise the reference may have a non-unit slope.

Choose a quantile convention

Software packages differ in how they interpolate between observations. Write down the convention when results will be compared across tools. Repeated values produce repeated or flat stretches; adding random jitter to hide ties changes the apparent pattern. For samples of different sizes, evaluate a common probability grid rather than aligning the first observation of each sorted list. Do not include probability zero or one in a theoretical distribution whose inverse CDF is infinite there. Box and violin views are useful companions when the Q–Q plot is too technical for a general audience.

Read center and tails separately

A nearly straight center with an upward bend in the high tail may indicate more large values in the vertical sample. A shift can move all points above the reference; a scale difference can change the slope. Avoid treating visual departures as an automatic hypothesis test. With a small sample, endpoints are unstable; with a huge sample, slight departures may be practically irrelevant. Sample-size uncertainty belongs in the caption. If the question is about service-level failures, count observations beyond a meaningful threshold as well as inspecting tail curvature.

Keep the comparison reproducible

Filter both samples by the same eligibility and time-window rules, then report their sizes and missing-value counts. If one group contains outages and the other excludes them, the plot is comparing policies as well as distributions. A chart export manifest should include filters, quantile grid, interpolation rule and transformed values. Provide a compact table of selected quantile pairs so a reader can inspect exact numbers without relying on hover or color. Never reverse the axes silently between reports.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def interpolate_quantile(sorted_values: list[float], probability: float) -> float:
    if not sorted_values or not 0 <= probability <= 1:
        raise ValueError("sample and probability are required")
    index = (len(sorted_values) - 1) * probability
    low = int(index)
    high = min(low + 1, len(sorted_values) - 1)
    return sorted_values[low] + (index - low) * (sorted_values[high] - sorted_values[low])

def paired_quantiles(reference: list[float], current: list[float],
                     probabilities: list[float]) -> list[tuple[float, float, float]]:
    if not reference or not current or any(not isfinite(value)
                                            for value in reference + current):
        raise ValueError("samples must contain finite values")
    if any(not 0 <= probability <= 1 for probability in probabilities):
        raise ValueError("probabilities must be inside zero and one")
    first, second = sorted(reference), sorted(current)
    return [(p, interpolate_quantile(first, p), interpolate_quantile(second, p))
            for p in probabilities]

quantile_pairs = paired_quantiles([47, 59, 81, 97, 113],
                                 [52, 61, 83, 101, 129], [0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
assert quantile_pairs == [(0.25, 59, 61), (0.5, 81, 83), (0.75, 97, 101)]

Performance and operating cost

Sorting reference and current samples of sizes A and B takes O(A log A + B log B) time; Q paired probabilities take O(Q) additional time and output space. The code uses linear interpolation at index (N minus one) times probability. It compares two empirical distributions, not a theoretical normal curve or a significance test. Preserve the method and sample sizes with the plot.

Common Mistakes

  • Pairing rows by index instead of pairing equal probabilities.
  • Switching interpolation methods between reports without disclosure.
  • Jittering ties until they look like genuine tail structure.
  • Calling every visible bend a statistically important deviation.

Validation drill

Compare 81 delivery-time records before and after a routing change. Plot common percentiles, report sample counts, and inspect whether the upper tail moved more than the median.

title: Empirical CDFs: read thresholds and tails without choosing bins
summary: Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.
body:
Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.

The step answers a threshold question

An empirical cumulative distribution function, or ECDF, gives the fraction of observed values less than or equal to each threshold. A point at 47 minutes and 0.8 means 80 percent of observations took at most 47 minutes. Unlike a histogram, it needs no bin width, so comparisons across groups are less sensitive to display choices. It still depends on the population, missing-value policy and observation window. Distribution plots should expose those rules before any percentile is interpreted.

Ties produce one jump

Repeated measurements at the same value create one larger step. If 31 of 81 jobs finish at exactly 12 minutes, the ECDF rises by 31/81 there; do not create a fake continuous slope between identical values. To compute a nearest-rank percentile, choose the first observed value whose cumulative share meets or exceeds the requested probability. Other quantile conventions interpolate and can return a number no job achieved. State the convention, especially for service targets. Sampling rules determine whether a percentile describes all jobs or a selected frame.

Keep the tail visible

Most observations can cluster near a short duration while a few long delays drive customer pain. An ECDF makes the proportion under a service threshold easy to read, but the far-right tail may still be squeezed by the axis. Add an inset, tail table or direct threshold counts when the rare cases matter. A survival-style complementary curve, one minus the ECDF, answers what fraction exceeds a threshold; be clear about strict versus inclusive inequalities at ties. Small samples need counts beside smooth-looking curves.

Compare only compatible cohorts

Two curves can differ because of case mix, eligibility, time window or measurement precision. Use consistent axis limits and units, label sample sizes, and show whether pending cases were excluded or censored. A naive ECDF of only completed jobs makes the slow unfinished work disappear. For a queue with unresolved jobs, use an analysis that handles censoring or restrict the claim to completed jobs. Observation status is part of the underlying data, not a cosmetic legend choice.

Worked contract

from math import ceil, isfinite

def completion_ecdf(minutes: list[float]) -> list[tuple[float, int, float]]:
    if not minutes or any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in minutes):
        raise ValueError("need finite nonnegative durations")
    ordered = sorted(minutes)
    steps = []
    for value in ordered:
        if steps and steps[-1][0] == value:
            steps[-1] = (value, steps[-1][1] + 1, 0.0)
        else:
            steps.append((value, 1, 0.0))
    cumulative = 0
    result = []
    for value, tied, _ in steps:
        cumulative += tied
        result.append((value, tied, cumulative / len(ordered)))
    return result

durations = [12, 12, 31, 47, 81]
curve = completion_ecdf(durations)
nearest_rank_80 = sorted(durations)[ceil(0.8 * len(durations)) - 1]
assert curve[0] == (12, 2, 0.4)
assert curve[-1][2] == 1.0 and nearest_rank_80 == 47

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N durations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) space for the ordered copy and output; scanning ties is O(N). Already-sorted warehouse output avoids the local sort. A chart with many distinct observations may still need visual reduction at screen resolution, but threshold queries should use the exact ordered values. The simple ECDF treats every supplied duration as complete and equally weighted; it is not a censored-data estimator.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a completed-only ECDF as the distribution of all started jobs.
  • Treating a large jump at a tied value as a renderer defect.
  • Quoting a percentile without its sample size and quantile convention.
  • Moving axis bounds between cohorts and comparing apparent steepness.

Validation drill

Build curves for two depot cohorts of 47 and 81 completed cases. Include repeated durations and unresolved work, then report the fraction within 31 minutes and exactly which cases were excluded.

title: Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
summary: A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.
body:
A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.

Show the independent count

Two channels can both report a 75 percent completion rate, yet one may have 12 receipts and another 12,000. Put eligible counts near marks or in an accessible companion table. If customers submit repeated receipts, the independent count may be customers rather than rows. Cluster resampling keeps those observations together.

Choose an interval contract

Specify the estimator, interval construction, confidence level and sampling unit. Error bars from an independent-row formula are misleading when assignments or outcomes cluster by reviewer. A confidence interval describes a repeated-sampling procedure; it is not a probability distribution over the displayed fixed rate. Coverage requires a valid observation process.

Separate overlap from decision

Overlapping intervals do not by themselves establish that a difference is absent, and nonoverlap is not a universal experiment test. If the task is to compare channels, calculate and display an interval for the difference under the study design. Pair this with practical limits: a two-point change may matter only above a declared volume or cost threshold.

Handle thin groups

A filter may leave one receipt or none. Use a visible “insufficient data” state rather than a narrow-looking point with absent error bars. Check that each interval is within the metric domain and that chart tooling does not clip it without notice. Keep the raw numerator and denominator available for audit.

Implementation

def interval_mark(point_rate, lower_rate, upper_rate, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 2:
        return {"state": "insufficient_data", "eligible_count": eligible_count}
    if not 0 <= lower_rate <= point_rate <= upper_rate <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid rate interval")
    return {"state": "measured", "point": point_rate,
            "lower": lower_rate, "upper": upper_rate, "eligible_count": eligible_count}

Performance and operating cost

Formatting M intervals is O(M) time and space. Interval estimation may be much more expensive, especially when resampling clusters; calculate it in a versioned data job and render the stored estimate with its construction metadata.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not draw error bars without naming their meaning.
  • Do not use receipt count as the independent sample size when customers repeat.
  • Do not interpret overlapping intervals as a complete test of a difference.

title: Distribution plots: keep the tail, missing values and bin policy visible
summary: Histograms and quantile summaries answer shape questions that a single mean or trend line cannot settle.
body:
Histograms and quantile summaries answer shape questions that a single mean or trend line cannot settle.

Distinguish populations

Review delay among completed receipts excludes receipts still open. A histogram of completed delays therefore cannot describe the full submission cohort without a censoring policy. State the population and cutoff. Distribution summaries help reveal a long tail, while a separate pending count shows records that do not yet have a delay.

Choose bins deliberately

A histogram with bins of one hour may appear noisy; a bin of one day can conceal a 24-hour service threshold. Fix bin edges across compared periods and label whether the left or right edge is included. Do not auto-bin each channel independently and then compare the resulting bar heights as though the units were identical.

Retain the tail

A rare 47-hour delay can matter more operationally than a high-volume cluster near five hours. If the axis is cropped to show the center, disclose the number above the cap and provide a full-range or quantile companion view. Invalid negative delays should be separated from valid extremes. Axis policy must remain stable across cohorts.

Make a small fixture

Start with delays of 3, 4, 5, 6 and 47 hours. The mean is 13 and the median is 5. A chart that omits the last value while still reporting the original mean is internally inconsistent. Test zero valid observations, one extreme observation and a delayed arrival that changes a closed reporting period.

Implementation

def delay_bins(delays_hours, edges):
    if len(edges) < 2 or edges[0] < 0 or any(left >= right for left, right in zip(edges, edges[1:])):
        raise ValueError("bin edges must increase from a nonnegative start")
    counts = [0] * (len(edges) - 1)
    overflow = 0
    for delay in delays_hours:
        if delay < edges[0]:
            raise ValueError("delay falls below the declared range")
        location = next((index for index, (left, right) in enumerate(zip(edges, edges[1:]))
                         if left <= delay < right), None)
        if location is None:
            overflow += 1
        else:
            counts[location] += 1
    return counts, overflow

Performance and operating cost

This direct bin search costs O(NB) for N observations and B bins, with O(B) output space. A binary search on sorted edges reduces lookup to O(N log B). Store missing and overflow counts separately so a faster renderer cannot erase them.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare histograms with different bin edges as if they were identical.
  • Do not trim a valid operational tail without reporting the omitted count.
  • Do not treat an unfinished receipt as a completed zero-hour delay.

title: Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
summary: A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.
body:
A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.

Fix the source grain

A receipt table can contain one row per receipt while a status log contains several rows per receipt. Joining them and counting rows creates a review volume that rises when the workflow emits more events. Reduce the log to one terminal outcome per receipt before joining, or build an explicit event-level chart. Join cardinality is a precondition for visual accuracy.

Choose the denominator

A chart titled “review completion rate” needs a rule for receipts that were submitted but not yet eligible, rejected at intake or still open. Keep numerator and denominator alongside the plotted rate in the data contract. When filtering by channel, recompute both counts for the filtered cohort; never filter precomputed overall rates and average them.

Control time bins

A daily chart needs one time zone, one interval convention and an explicit policy for late events. A receipt submitted at 23:58 and completed after midnight might belong to the submission-day cohort even though its completion event occurs next day. Calendar policy keeps those two clocks apart. Document whether incomplete days are omitted or shown as provisional.

Reconcile the visual

For two channels with 34 of 47 and 18 of 23 timely receipts, the combined rate is 52 of 70, about 74.3 percent. The simple average of the two channel percentages is different. Test that the dashboard total uses summed counts. Include an empty group and one duplicated receipt ID to catch silent inflation.

Implementation

def weighted_completion_rate(channel_counts):
    timely = 0
    eligible = 0
    for timely_count, eligible_count in channel_counts:
        if not 0 <= timely_count <= eligible_count:
            raise ValueError("invalid channel counts")
        timely += timely_count
        eligible += eligible_count
    return None if eligible == 0 else timely / eligible

Performance and operating cost

Aggregating N rows by C keys is O(N) expected time and O(C) state with a hash map. Sorting labels adds O(C log C). A database group-by can move the work closer to the source, but its join and filter contracts still need inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not average percentages when group sizes differ.
  • Do not count event rows as independent receipts.
  • Do not combine submission and completion timestamps without a cohort rule.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
summary: Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.
body:
Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.

A symbol has a location contract

A circle over a map may represent a precise facility, a regional centroid or an approximate address. Those are not equivalent. State what the coordinate means and how much location precision the data support. Choropleth maps color whole regions; proportional symbols encode a value at a point or chosen anchor. Do not place a regional total at a centroid without telling the reader that the circle summarizes an area. If location is sensitive, aggregate or coarsen before publication rather than relying on small marker size to conceal it.

Area should represent quantity

If a symbol encodes a nonnegative count, its visual area should be proportional to that count. Doubling the radius multiplies area by four, exaggerating the larger value. Compute radius from the square root of value relative to a declared maximum. Use a visible reference legend with at least two example magnitudes. A zero count should remain a recorded zero, even if its circle has no area; a tiny outline or table entry may be needed to keep the location discoverable. Scale integrity also means fixing the size domain across maps intended for comparison.

Overlapping circles need an explicit policy

Dense areas can hide smaller symbols under larger ones. Drawing order, opacity and zoom can all change what a reader sees. Try smaller maximum radius, outlines, clustering with disclosed counts, or an alternate ranked table. Do not let overlap remove records from the export. Hexbin density may be better when the question is where point events concentrate, while a proportional-symbol map is better when each point already has a meaningful aggregate. Test overlapping facilities at the closest supported zoom and on a narrow phone viewport.

Count and rate are different maps

A large population center may dominate a count map while having a modest per-person rate. A rate can be mapped with symbol size only if the legend names its denominator and the sampling uncertainty is not buried. Often a count-sized symbol plus a separately encoded rate is too much for one map; use paired maps or a table. The denominator contract must follow the geography and period. Export ID, coordinate meaning, count, denominator, computed rate, symbol radius and suppression state, so the map can be checked without its pixels.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def area_scaled_radii(values: dict[str, float],
                      maximum_radius: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    if not isfinite(maximum_radius) or maximum_radius <= 0:
        raise ValueError("maximum radius must be positive")
    if not values or any(not place for place in values):
        raise ValueError("locations must be named")
    if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in values.values()):
        raise ValueError("mapped values must be finite and nonnegative")
    maximum_value = max(values.values())
    if maximum_value == 0:
        return {place: 0.0 for place in values}
    return {place: maximum_radius * sqrt(value / maximum_value)
            for place, value in values.items()}

service_calls = {"north depot": 47, "south depot": 188, "west depot": 0}
radii = area_scaled_radii(service_calls, 20)
assert radii["south depot"] == 20
assert radii["north depot"] == 10
assert radii["west depot"] == 0

Performance and operating cost

For N locations, finding the maximum and calculating radii takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code sizes nonnegative values by area and leaves geographic projection, collision handling and legend generation to the map renderer. A production map must keep one fixed reference maximum across views that readers are expected to compare; recalculating it after every filter changes apparent size.

Common Mistakes

  • Making radius proportional to count and thereby exaggerating area.
  • Treating a regional centroid as an exact event location.
  • Letting large symbols cover small ones without a table or overlap strategy.
  • Comparing maps whose size domains were auto-scaled independently.

Validation drill

Map 59 service depots with zero, small and large call counts. Use area-scaled circles, disclose the location meaning and produce a fixed-size legend for two reporting periods.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

Validation drill

Facet five depot delay series on one weekly calendar. Produce a shared-scale view for absolute comparison and a labeled independent-scale view for within-depot variation; write down which conclusions differ.

title: Seasonal subseries plots: compare the same cycle position across years
summary: Group repeated cycle positions, draw their chronological traces and calculate reference means only from complete cycles.
body:
Group repeated cycle positions, draw their chronological traces and calculate reference means only from complete cycles.

Choose a cycle for a real operational reason

A seasonal subseries plot groups observations by their position within a known repeating cycle: all first quarters together, all second quarters together and so on. Within each group, preserve chronological order across cycles and draw a reference mean or median for that position. The view exposes both differences between cycle positions and changes within one position over years. A quarterly series needs four positions; a weekly schedule might need seven weekdays. Do not infer the cycle merely because a pattern looks attractive after trying many candidates. Document the calendar origin and whether a period is a full business day, fiscal week or standard month. Autocorrelation plots can suggest repetition, but their lag peaks do not supply the business calendar. Time-series calendar rules fix the period definitions.

Align like positions and keep the trend visible

A quarter-one rise across years can coexist with quarter three being the seasonal high. If the group means are calculated over the entire time span, a rising long-term trend can make later years look elevated at every position and exaggerate a seasonal story. Inspect the original chronological series and, when justified, a separately labeled detrended view. Do not quietly subtract a trend and publish the adjusted trace as raw volume. The seasonal subseries plot is descriptive; a repeated peak does not establish that the calendar position causes it. Keep all panels on one vertical scale so a small within-quarter change is not magnified by a custom axis. Shared-scale panels and event annotations make context visible without overclaiming.

Do not let an unfinished cycle define the reference

A current year with only two complete quarters can contribute those two observed points, but it must not be treated as a four-quarter baseline. Mark its unobserved quarters as missing, not zero, and freeze the complete historical cycles used for the reference means. A backfilled quarter can change the baseline; version that change. The code below requires each reference cycle to contain every position once and permits a later incomplete cycle for display only. Real calendar data also need an explicit policy for holidays, leap days, 53-week years and corrected reports. Counts behind averages belong in the accompanying table. Calendar completeness and missing-cell encoding apply when the same data is shown as a matrix.

Make the grouped view answer a concrete question

For capacity planning, ask whether the same quarter reliably peaks, whether peak magnitude is changing and whether the latest complete point is unusual relative to its own season. A grouped trace can reveal that a conventional time-series line obscures those comparisons. Yet two historical cycles are weak evidence of recurrence; unusual one-off events can dominate a group mean. Show the exact number of complete cycles, use a median reference when outliers are common and inspect sensitivity to leaving out a cycle. Do not project the group mean forward as a forecast without an evaluated model and uncertainty. Forecast fan charts have that different purpose. Provide labels and a reference table for readers who cannot distinguish traces by color alone; accessible chart guidance covers the contract.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict
from math import isfinite

def seasonal_subseries(readings: list[tuple[int, int, float]],
                       positions: int, last_reference_cycle: int):
    if positions < 2 or not isinstance(last_reference_cycle, int):
        raise ValueError("declare cycle length and reference cutoff")
    by_position = defaultdict(list)
    seen = set()
    reference_cycles = set()
    for cycle, position, volume in readings:
        if (not isinstance(cycle, int) or not isinstance(position, int) or
                not 1 <= position <= positions or not isfinite(volume) or
                (cycle, position) in seen):
            raise ValueError("cycle positions must be unique, valid and finite")
        seen.add((cycle, position))
        by_position[position].append((cycle, volume))
        if cycle <= last_reference_cycle:
            reference_cycles.add(cycle)
    if not reference_cycles or any(
            (cycle, position) not in seen
            for cycle in reference_cycles for position in range(1, positions + 1)):
        raise ValueError("every reference cycle must be complete")
    result = []
    for position in range(1, positions + 1):
        trace = sorted(by_position[position])
        reference = [volume for cycle, volume in trace
                     if cycle in reference_cycles]
        result.append((position, len(reference), sum(reference) / len(reference), trace))
    return result

quarterly_orders = [(47, 1, 47), (47, 2, 59), (47, 3, 83), (47, 4, 71),
                    (48, 1, 59), (48, 2, 71), (48, 3, 97), (48, 4, 83),
                    (49, 1, 61), (49, 2, 73)]
panels = seasonal_subseries(quarterly_orders, positions=4,
                            last_reference_cycle=48)
assert panels[0] == (1, 2, 53.0, [(47, 47), (48, 59), (49, 61)])
assert panels[2] == (3, 2, 90.0, [(47, 83), (48, 97)])
assert panels[3][3] == [(47, 71), (48, 83)]

Performance and operating cost

For N readings, validation and grouping take O(N) expected time; sorting each position's trace costs O(sum nₛ log nₛ), bounded by O(N log N). Checking reference completeness takes O(C·S) for C reference cycles and S positions. Stored traces and the duplicate-key set need O(N) space. The toy quarterly ledger uses two complete reference years, giving a first-quarter mean of 53 orders and a third-quarter mean of 90. The partial third year appears only where observed, and never changes the frozen reference. Two cycles verify code behavior but cannot establish dependable seasonality.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting the four-position cycle at the wrong fiscal quarter.
  • Treating an unobserved current-quarter cell as a measured zero.
  • Mixing a trend-adjusted trace with raw-volume reference means without labeling the change.
  • Calling a cycle-position mean a validated forecast or causal explanation.

Validation drill

Take 47 completed fiscal years with four quarters each and one partial current year. Audit duplicate and missing quarter keys, show chronological traces for each quarter, calculate references only from complete years, and compare the grouped view with the ungrouped time series.
